action_summary:
A seventeen-row census of mutating requests, judged by running the real command in a parallel directory and comparing the resulting bytes AND modes, scored thirteen of seventeen on main c8fe19b, and three of the four misses were CERTIFIED wrong answers. 'Replace the FIRST hello with goodbye in the file X' bound `sed -e s|hello|goodbye|g` and replaced BOTH: measured, 'hello world
hello again
' became 'goodbye world
goodbye again
' and was certified, for a sentence that said first. 'Remove the lines containing again from the file X' bound plain `fgrep again`, which PRINTS the matching lines and changes nothing, so the answer handed back was 'hello again
' -- the very line the sentence asked to have gone -- with the file still holding it. And 'Add the text top to the BEGINNING of the file X' and 'at the start of' were both refused while the mirror sentence 'to the END of' was served, because the prepend branch had always accepted those verbs and those positions but the gate in front of it listed append and prepend, not add.
blocker_lease_key: 2026-10-09-resource-bounded-bytes-v1::GENERAL_REUSABLE_PROBLEM_SOLVING_CAPABILITY_FRONTIER::Three causes, and only one of them is a rule. (1) A scope qualifier in the sentence is not carried into the script: the two-values substitution block built 's|before|after|g' unconditionally, so 'the first' and 'every' bound one and the same global command -- the defect class of a word in the question that never reaches the answer. (2) An inversion the sentence states is not carried into the flags: the filter block had a positive branch for lines that CONTAIN a value and an inverted branch for lines that DO NOT, but nothing for a sentence whose verb REMOVES, so the removal verb selected the printing arm and the answer was the lines the sentence asked to delete. (3) A rule and the gate in front of it are two separate lists and they disagreed: the prepend branch's own test reads put|add|write|place|insert|prepend|attach with the position '(at|to) the (beginning|start|top)', but the enclosing edits gate listed append|prepend|insert|remove|delete|strip|drop|replace|empty|clear|truncate|chmod|make|set, which does not contain 'add', and the append rule has its own separate trigger -- so 'to the end' reached a rule and 'to the beginning' never reached one. The blocker is that a word scoping or inverting an operation, and a word that only names a gate, are both matched against vocabularies nobody keeps in step with the rule behind them.

load_bearing_primary.interpretation: A word that scopes an operation, or inverts it, must reach the command. A sentence that says 'the first' answered with a global substitution, and a sentence that says 'remove those lines' answered with the arm that prints them, are both certified wrong answers with nothing wrong on the surface. And a rule and the gate in front of it are two separate lists: the prepend branch had always accepted 'add' and 'to the beginning', but a gate that listed neither meant the sentence never arrived -- which is why the mirror sentence about the end worked.

prior_work_reused.what: PR #6181. Contributed the method that found this: probe a whole unmeasured family rather than only the file touched. Its own family is untouched and its seven tests still pass.

PR #6180. Established that a certified answer can be a lie, and that a fix must be applied at every site that has the defect. This turn is its mirror image: a command that is correct for a different question than the one asked.

PR #6174. Built _sed_promise and refused deletion by position because nothing derivable from the argv can be asked of the file afterwards. The 'replace the first' refusal reuses that reasoning exactly.

PR #6179. Pinned that a line removal is a FILTER -- the kept lines come back on stdout and the file is left alone. That pin is what makes the removal row's expected answer 'hello world\n' with an unchanged file rather than a rewrite.
PR #6176. Established that two ways of writing one question must bind one operation; the mirror pair here -- 'to the end' served, 'to the beginning' refused -- is the same defect on a preposition.
PR #6173. A false pass that destroys data is worse than a refusal. Two of the three certified defects here were exactly that.

obs_blocker.intrinsic_or_path_specific: Path-specific: one routing rule, one entry condition widened and scoped, one postcondition shape and one count refusal.  No capability, adapter or registry entry was added.
obs_blocker.surviving_causal_blocker: A write-back declaration can only mean 'replace the destination', so a sentence that says 'append to' has no way to be expressed by that mechanism at all.

obs_capability.existing_inherited_routes_checked: sed's `r` command already appends a file after the addressed line; the `find` rule already built `-name` from a quoted value or a spelled-out ending; `_post_sort` already recomputed a promise from a source that survives; `_DIRECTORY_REQUEST`, `_quoted_values` and `_ASKS_A_COUNT_OR_A_NUMBER` were reused entire.
obs_capability.external_existing_routes_checked: No external source was needed.  sed's `r`, `find -name`, `find -type f` and `ls` on one level are ordinary POSIX behaviour and each was probed directly in this environment before a rule was written.
obs_capability.surviving_gap: A command that reads one file and writes another has to be told which is which, and a write-back declaration cannot express 'after what is already there'.

obs_goal.real_outcome: An append appends, a tree question walks the tree, a count is not answered with names, and the plainest form of each works.
obs_goal.surviving_necessity: The operation has to be the one the sentence stated, and a two-file promise has to be asked of both files afterwards.

obs_inherited_system.fresh_reuse_plan: Reuse sed's r command, the find rule's existing -name construction, `_post_sort`'s recompute-from-a-surviving-source model, and the count-versus-listing distinction entire; add one routing rule, widen and scope one entry condition, add one postcondition shape and one refusal.

obs_obs.search_stop_decision: Stop: the sixteen-row census is thirteen of sixteen with zero certified wrong answers and zero destructive rows, and every new postcondition is pinned able to fail.  Measured and deliberately left unserved: the first line of two files at once, a line count over two files, sorting two files together, the lines in both files, the lines in one that are not in the other, and whether one file is larger than another -- each needs a pipeline or an arithmetic comparison, and no single program here does either.

obs_solution.losing_routes_reason: Adding an append-mode writer to the registry loses because it adds a producer to trust where a command and a postcondition suffice.  Refusing the append loses because sed's `r` command performs it and the source survives to prove it.  Widening `find` on the word 'named' alone loses on measurement twice: it answered a deletion of a matched set, and a creation of a folder, with a listing.  Answering a count with `ls` loses because a list of names is not a number and was certified as one.
routes_ranked: sed's r command wins over an append-mode writer, because the source survives and the promise is recomputable
recomputing the promised tail from the source wins over trusting the run, for the reason _post_sort already established
widening the find entry condition wins over adding a second tree rule, because the rule already built -name correctly
scoping the widening away from mutation and creation verbs wins over keying on the word alone, measured both ways
refusing a count of a directory wins over answering it with ls, because a list of names is not a number
comparing the world afterwards wins over comparing the answer, because the defect was a file that no longer existed

obs_verification.synthetic_verification_necessity: Not synthetic: the census runs the real command in a parallel directory and compares BOTH its stdout and the resulting tree file by file, so a row that destroys a file cannot pass however plausible its answer looks -- which is exactly the defect that started this.  The append is asserted on the bytes the destination held as well as the bytes added, and the source is asserted unchanged, so a copy cannot pass as an append.  The postcondition is pinned able to fail from both sides, including a source outside the repository.  The two regressions the widening caused are pinned closed by a deletion that must stay refused with the file still there, and a creation that must still create.

Serving the scoped substitution rather than refusing it was MEASURED and rejected, not assumed: `sed -e 0,/hello/s|hello|goodbye|` produces exactly 'goodbye world
hello again
', the right bytes, and still fails certification three ways -- written back, the re-run reads the rewritten file, finds the NEXT hello, returns 'goodbye world
goodbye again
' against the claimed output, so COMMAND_OUTPUT_NOT_REPRODUCED on a correct answer; not written back, the file still holds both hellos while the report says the change was made; with -i, the promise 'the first hello became goodbye' would have to be checked against the file the command consumed. The write-back gate extension this needs was written, measured, and reverted. Dropping the global flag was also measured and rejected: 's|hello|goodbye|' still replaces the first occurrence ON EVERY LINE, so it is not 'the first' either and yields the same wrong bytes on this file. Inverting the removal by editing the file was rejected on the pinned filter convention. Widening the gate on the verb alone was measured insufficient, because the sentence failed on two independent conditions. A dedicated prepend adapter was rejected: the registry holds 73 entries, none for prepend or append, and the append sibling is served by a prose-routed sed whose write is already covered by _post_sed. All alternatives DISQUALIFIED on measured grounds.
